People judge. This makes their judgment traceable.
Every rating traces back to something a real evaluator saw and wrote down at the time they saw it, checked against a rubric people wrote in advance, and ratified by a person before it reaches anyone.
A busy workshop makes it easy for real observations to be forgotten. Feedback arrives too late to act on, and the final judgment rests on whoever happened to remember the most at the end.

On the fly, ad hoc, lost
Two workshops side by side: one where observations scatter and are lost, one where they are recorded, verified, and compiled into reports.
The AI is a clerk, not a judge

It has one narrow job: take the free-form notes a facilitator writes while watching an activity and turn them into tidy observations, each tied to a specific skill and a specific piece of evidence. It does not decide a score on its own. It does not invent evidence. Nothing reaches a participant or their organization until a person has read it.
Every rating traces to a specific, timestamped observation.
You can always walk back from a score to the reason for it.
No draft is final until a person checks it against the evidence and approves it.
When two evaluators see someone differently, that is surfaced and worked out by people, not averaged away.
